actions.name: Home vital signs (temperature, HR, BP, RR)

actions.name: Camera inspection of sacral skin (patient/girlfriend-assisted, using mirror or phone photo)
actions.result: 2.5 cm area over sacrum: skin intact but with partial-thickness loss of dermis, pink-red wound bed, no slough, surrounding skin mildly erythematous, no drainage visible, no odor reported by patient — consistent with Stage 2 pressure injury

actions.name: Guided spasticity exam (patient performs passive leg movement, reports resistance and spasm frequency)
actions.result: Increased resistance to passive knee extension bilaterally with 3-4 beats of clonus noted on guided exam; patient separately reports 15-20 spasms/day, several nocturnal, interfering with transfers and sleep. Note: formal Modified Ashworth Scale grading requires in-person clinician palpation of resistance through range of motion and cannot be reliably assigned by patient-report alone; clonus and spasm frequency are not MAS components

actions.name: Camera inspection of lower extremities for swelling, color, skin breakdown elsewhere
actions.result: No calf swelling or asymmetry, no other skin breakdown noted on thighs, feet, or heels on camera

actions.name: Review of home bladder catheterization log
actions.result: Log shows intermittent catheterization performed only 1.9-2.3 times per day on average over the last 3 weeks, well below the prescribed goal of every 4-6 hours (4x daily)

actions.name: Review bowel program log
actions.result: Bowel program log shows bowel movements every 3-4 days (goal every 1-2 days), several entries note hard stool requiring prolonged time and manual disimpaction by caregiver

actions.name: Review outpatient PT/OT attendance record
actions.result: No outpatient therapy visits logged in the last 10 weeks; last attended session 10 weeks ago. Prior note documents transportation barrier reported by patient (unreliable paratransit van)

actions.name: Review current medication list
actions.result: Baclofen 10 mg PO three times daily (unchanged x6 months); no PRN analgesic or stool softener currently prescribed; no antibiotics on list

actions.name: Order/review urinalysis with microscopy and urine culture (via home health or local lab draw)
actions.result: See lab report: urinalysis shows pyuria and bacteriuria; culture pending at time of visit, to be followed up

actions.name: PHQ-9 depression screen (administered verbally)
actions.result: Score 14/27, consistent with moderate depressive symptoms; endorses low energy, poor sleep (confounded by spasms), feelings of being a burden, denies active suicidal ideation

actions.name: Functional mobility/transfer self-report (modified FIM-type questions)
actions.result: Reports transfers (bed-to-chair, chair-to-car) now take longer and require more upper body effort due to leg spasms; one near-fall from wheelchair during transfer in last week; otherwise independent with wheelchair mobility on level surfaces

actions.name: Camera inspection of wheelchair cushion and seating setup
actions.result: Patient shows a gel cushion that appears compressed/worn at center; patient reports it is the original cushion issued 8 months ago, has not been reassessed by seating clinic since discharge

actions.name: Home blood glucose check (patient has home glucometer)
actions.result: Fasting glucose 92 mg/dL, reported from home glucometer

actions.name: Review autonomic/vital sign log for episodes of autonomic dysreflexia
actions.result: No episodes of severe headache, flushing, or sudden hypertension logged; patient denies classic autonomic dysreflexia symptoms despite bladder/bowel issues, though low-grade dysreflexia cannot be excluded by history alone

actions.name: Review driving evaluation / vocational rehabilitation referral status
actions.result: No driving evaluation or vocational rehabilitation referral on file since initial discharge planning 8 months ago

artifacts.title: Inpatient Rehabilitation Discharge Summary (8 months ago)
artifacts.author: Inpatient Rehabilitation Attending
artifacts.body: 33-year-old man with T10 AIS A complete paraplegia after motorcycle collision (T9-T10 burst fracture, s/p posterior spinal fusion). Discharged home with manual wheelchair, independent with intermittent catheterization technique (taught goal: every 4-6 hours, 4x/day) and bowel program (goal: every 1-2 days using suppository/digital stimulation). Baclofen 10 mg TID initiated for lower extremity spasticity. Plan: outpatient PT/OT twice weekly, seating clinic follow-up at 6 months, driving evaluation and vocational rehabilitation referral to be arranged as outpatient. Patient was independent with wheelchair mobility and transfers at discharge, cushion issued was standard gel cushion pending seating clinic customization.

facts.chart: Reports 3 weeks of worsening bilateral lower extremity spasms, now 15-20/day including nocturnal episodes, interfering with transfers and sleep
facts.says: My legs have been jumping around so much the last few weeks, it's throwing off my transfers and waking me up at night.

facts.chart: Reports spasms worse with sitting too long and at night, no clear position that fully relieves them
facts.says: They're worse if I've been sitting a long time, and they hit me hard right when I'm trying to fall asleep.

facts.chart: Reports one near-fall from wheelchair during a transfer in the past week due to a spasm
facts.says: Last week I almost went straight out of my chair during a transfer, my leg just locked up on me.

facts.chart: Takes baclofen 10 mg three times daily as prescribed, has not missed doses, no dose change in 6 months
facts.says: I take my baclofen pills, three times a day, every day, same as always.

facts.chart: T10 AIS A complete paraplegia from motorcycle crash 8 months ago, s/p spinal fusion
facts.says: I broke my back in a motorcycle wreck eight months ago, they put rods in, and I haven't been able to move my legs since.

facts.chart: Reports urine has looked cloudy and smelled strong/foul for the past 1-2 weeks
facts.says: My pee's been looking cloudy and it smells pretty bad lately, worse than normal.

facts.chart: Reports feeling warm and tired the last couple days, no measured fever at home until today's visit
facts.says: I've felt kind of hot and run down the last day or two, didn't think much of it.

facts.chart: Admits to performing intermittent catheterization about 2 times per day rather than the prescribed 4 times per day, citing being busy and sometimes forgetting
facts.says: Honestly I've been doing it like twice a day instead of four times, I just get busy and forget, or I'm not near a bathroom.

facts.chart: Bowel movements occurring every 3-4 days, stools hard, requires prolonged time and occasional manual assistance from girlfriend
facts.says: My bowels have been real irregular, maybe every three or four days, and it's hard and takes forever to get anything out.

facts.chart: Girlfriend noticed a reddened open area on his sacrum about one week ago; patient was unaware until she pointed it out
facts.says: My girlfriend saw something back there about a week ago and told me, I can't really see it myself.

facts.chart: Patient reluctantly agrees to show a photo of the sacral area taken by his girlfriend after being asked directly
facts.says: I guess I can show you the picture she took, it's kind of embarrassing but here.

facts.chart: Reports inconsistent weight shifts, sometimes going 2-3 hours without shifting especially when busy or distracted
facts.says: I know I'm supposed to shift my weight every so often but some days I just forget and sit for a couple hours straight.

facts.chart: Using original gel cushion issued at discharge 8 months ago; never reassessed by seating clinic
facts.says: This is the same cushion they gave me when I left the hospital, nobody's looked at it since.

facts.chart: Stopped attending outpatient PT/OT about 10 weeks ago after repeated transportation failures with paratransit van service
facts.says: I stopped going to therapy a couple months back, that van service kept not showing up or showing up so late it wasn't worth it.

facts.chart: Reports low mood, low energy, feeling like a burden on girlfriend, denies suicidal ideation when asked directly
facts.says: Some days I just feel like a burden on her, like I'm not pulling my weight anymore. But I'm not thinking about hurting myself or anything like that.

facts.chart: Reports poor sleep over past 3 weeks, attributes it to nighttime spasms waking him multiple times per night
facts.says: I'm barely sleeping, these spasms wake me up two three times a night.

facts.chart: Asks about getting evaluated for hand-control driving so he can be more independent
facts.says: I keep hearing about these hand controls for driving, I want to know how I get set up for that.

facts.chart: Expresses strong desire to return to work as an electrician's apprentice or find a related vocational path
facts.says: I was almost done with my apprenticeship, I really want to find a way back to that kind of work, or something close to it.

facts.chart: Lives with girlfriend who assists with some care tasks; home has one step at entrance, bathroom not fully modified
facts.says: I'm staying with my girlfriend, she helps me out when she can, but our place still has a step to get in and the bathroom's not really set up for me.

facts.chart: Denies severe headache, sudden sweating, flushing, or episodes of markedly elevated blood pressure
facts.says: I haven't had any sudden bad headaches or sweating spells or anything like that.

facts.chart: Denies new back pain or neurological level change; reports only spasm-related discomfort in legs
facts.says: My back feels the same as always, it's really just my legs jumping that's bothering me.

facts.chart: Denies redness or breakdown at heels, ischial areas, or elbows on his own inspection
facts.says: My heels and the rest of me seem okay as far as I can tell.

facts.chart: Drinks alcohol socially, about 2-3 beers on weekends, denies daily use
facts.says: I'll have a couple beers on the weekend with friends, nothing heavy.

facts.chart: Father has type 2 diabetes, no family history of neurological or autoimmune disease
facts.says: My dad's got diabetes, but nobody in the family has anything like what happened to me.

facts.says: I probably don't drink enough water, maybe a few cups a day, and I eat a lot of fast food since cooking's hard for me now.

facts.says: I've started doing my transfers different, trying to muscle through with my arms more since my legs just go crazy if I set them down wrong.

facts.says: Some days I just don't do the whole bowel routine, especially if I'm tired or in a rush.

facts.says: I don't think I'm leaking more than usual, but honestly I'm not catheterizing enough to really know.

facts.chart: Reports spasms have worsened despite no change in baclofen dose or timing, suspects something else is going on
facts.says: I'm taking the same baclofen I always have, same amount, so I don't get why it's suddenly so much worse.

objectives.text: Identify untreated urinary tract infection as a likely driver of worsened spasticity in a patient with spinal cord injury, linking catheterization non-adherence to clinical findings.
Detect and stage a pressure injury via remote camera/photo examination despite patient reluctance to disclose it, and connect it to inconsistent weight-shifting and an overdue wheelchair cushion.

Recognize noxious stimuli below the level of injury (UTI, pressure injury, constipation, bladder distension) as common secondary causes of worsened spasticity in spinal cord injury, rather than attributing the change solely to baclofen inadequacy.

Screen for and address psychosocial barriers to rehabilitation participation, including depression and transportation access, and plan appropriate referral rather than managing mood disorder independently.

Counsel on vocational and driving goals within physiatry scope, directing to appropriate driving rehabilitation and vocational rehabilitation referral pathways rather than making those determinations directly.
Identify a mismatch between patient-reported medication/self-care adherence and objective home monitoring logs, and use it as a nonjudgmental teaching opportunity rather than confrontation.

answerKey.primaryProblem: Worsening lower-extremity spasticity in chronic complete T10 paraplegia, most likely triggered by an untreated urinary tract infection in the setting of under-frequent intermittent catheterization, compounded by constipation and an evolving stage 2 sacral pressure injury (all acting as noxious stimuli below the injury level).
differential: Urinary tract infection acting as noxious stimulus worsening spasticity (most likely)
Evolving pressure injury as a second noxious stimulus contributing to spasticity
Constipation/fecal loading as a contributing noxious stimulus
Baclofen tolerance or need for dose adjustment (less likely given no dose change history and clear alternate triggers)
Early autonomic dysreflexia (screened for, not currently supported by history)

Syrinx or new structural spinal cord pathology (less likely in absence of sensory level change or new pain, but should remain on differential if spasticity does not improve after treating reversible triggers)
keyFindings: 3-week history of markedly increased spasm frequency (15-20/day) with nocturnal spasms and a near-fall during transfer
Catheterization performed only ~2x/day versus prescribed 4-6x/day goal, with cloudy foul-smelling urine
Urinalysis positive for pyuria, bacteriuria, and nitrites; culture pending
Low-grade subjective fever/malaise reported, temperature 100.6°F on home vitals
Stage 2 sacral pressure injury identified only after direct, reluctant disclosure and photo review
Inconsistent weight shifts (every 2-3 hours instead of recommended frequent shifts) and an 8-month-old, non-reassessed wheelchair cushion
Bowel movements every 3-4 days with hard stools and inconsistent adherence to bowel program
10 weeks without outpatient therapy due to unreliable paratransit, with no interim equipment/seating reassessment
PHQ-9 score of 14 (moderate depression) with feelings of being a burden, no active suicidal ideation
Mismatch: patient reports taking baclofen reliably and implies routine care is on track, but home logs show catheterization and bowel program adherence well below prescribed goals
plan: Treat suspected urinary tract infection: coordinate urine culture follow-up and antibiotic initiation per primary care/urology per local protocol; physiatry to flag urgency given spasticity impact and SCI context
Reinforce and retrain intermittent catheterization technique and frequency goal (every 4-6 hours), problem-solve real-world barriers (schedule, bathroom access) with nursing/case management support
Initiate structured bowel program adherence support (consistent timing, adequate fluid/fiber intake) and consider need for bowel regimen adjustment in conjunction with primary care

Manage stage 2 sacral pressure injury with offloading education, wound care instructions, and refer to wound care/home health nursing for monitoring; address with increased weight-shift frequency education
Refer to seating/wheelchair clinic for cushion reassessment given 8 months of use without re-evaluation and new skin breakdown

Address transportation barrier to outpatient therapy; coordinate with case management/social work for reliable transport solution (e.g., alternate paratransit authorization, telerehabilitation sessions) and restart PT/OT
Refer for formal mental health evaluation/counseling given PHQ-9 of 14 with psychosocial stressors; physiatry to monitor but not manage depression treatment independently
Refer to driving rehabilitation program for formal hand-control driving evaluation
Refer to vocational rehabilitation services to explore return-to-work options, potentially including accommodated electrical trade work or related vocational paths
Hold current baclofen dose unchanged for now; reassess spasticity severity after treating infection, skin, and bowel issues before considering spasticity medication escalation
Schedule close follow-up (1-2 weeks) to reassess spasticity, skin, urinary and bowel status, and mood after interventions
redFlags: Near-fall from wheelchair during transfer due to spasm — safety risk requiring prompt action
Fever and malaise in a person with spinal cord injury and suspected UTI — risk of ascending infection/urosepsis if untreated
Pressure injury with signs of surrounding erythema — risk of progression if offloading and wound care not promptly addressed
PHQ-9 score of 14 with reports of feeling like a burden — monitor for worsening depression; emergent reassessment needed if suicidal ideation emerges
New or worsening spasticity in SCI should always prompt screening for occult noxious stimuli (bladder, bowel, skin) before assuming medication-related causes
educationPoints: Sudden worsening of spasticity in spinal cord injury is a common clinical clue to an occult noxious stimulus below the level of injury (infection, bladder distension, bowel impaction, skin breakdown) rather than primary spasticity medication failure
Routine, nonjudgmental screening for catheterization and bowel program adherence is essential, since objective logs may reveal gaps that patients may not fully recognize or may underreport

Pressure injuries can be missed by patients themselves, especially over the sacrum, making camera-assisted or caregiver-assisted skin checks and direct, respectful questioning important in telehealth SCI follow-up

Physiatry plays a coordinating role for driving evaluation, vocational rehabilitation, mental health referral, and durable medical equipment reassessment rather than independently managing all these domains
Transportation barriers are a common and modifiable cause of rehabilitation therapy non-adherence that should be proactively addressed by the care team

mismatches.patientClaim: Patient states he takes baclofen as prescribed and, when asked generally about his self-care, conveys that his catheterization routine is on track since nothing has changed recently.
mismatches.recordEvidence: Home catheterization frequency trend chart shows average of only 1.9-2.3 catheterizations per day over the past 3 weeks, well below the prescribed goal of 4-6 times daily, correlating with the onset of cloudy, foul-smelling urine.
mismatches.teachingPoint: Patients may sincerely believe their self-care routine is adequate or unchanged while objective logs reveal a gradual drift from prescribed frequency; reviewing home monitoring data is essential before attributing new symptoms solely to disease progression or medication failure.

mismatches.patientClaim: Patient initially states that his skin seems okay everywhere as far as he can tell, including by self-inspection.
mismatches.recordEvidence: Patient-submitted photo (reviewed after direct, reluctant disclosure) shows a 2.5 cm Stage 2 pressure injury over the sacrum with surrounding erythema, an area the patient cannot visually inspect himself.
mismatches.teachingPoint: Self-report of skin integrity is unreliable for areas like the sacrum that patients with SCI cannot see or feel; routine camera-assisted or caregiver-assisted skin checks over high-risk pressure points should be built into every follow-up visit regardless of patient reassurance.

patient.name: Jamal Edwards
patient.occupation: Former electrician's apprentice, currently not working
patient.appearance: A well-built man in his early thirties with short cropped hair, wearing a plain gray t-shirt, seated in his manual wheelchair in what looks like a modest living room with a couch visible behind him. His expression is guarded and tired at the start of the call, arms resting on his wheelchair armrests, and he glances off-camera occasionally as if checking for his girlfriend nearby.

persona.personality: Proud, self-reliant, and initially guarded about anything that feels like a personal failure or embarrassment; underneath that, practical and motivated to solve problems once he trusts the clinician is not judging him.
persona.communicationStyle: Speaks in short, direct sentences at first; opens up with more detail and emotion once rapport is established; uses plain, everyday language, not medical terms.
persona.emotionalState: Tired, somewhat frustrated and low in mood, with underlying worry about his safety during transfers and his future; brightens slightly when discussing driving and work goals.
persona.background: Jamal was nearly finished with his electrician's apprenticeship in Memphis when a motorcycle crash eight months ago left him paralyzed from the chest down. He now lives with his girlfriend, who has become his main support person. He grew up in Memphis, has a close relationship with a couple of old coworkers but has drifted from extended family since the accident, and used to enjoy working on cars and listening to music in his free time.
speechExamples: I'm not trying to make a big deal out of nothing, but these spasms have gotten bad.
It's embarrassing, but I guess I should just tell you about it.
I used to be the guy fixing things, now I feel like I can't even fix my own body.
I just want to know if I can get back to some kind of work, even if it's not exactly the same as before.
concerns: Worried the spasms mean something is seriously wrong or getting worse
Embarrassed about the pressure sore and catheter habits, afraid of being judged
Anxious about safety during transfers after the near-fall
Wants practical answers about driving with hand controls and returning to work
Feels guilty about relying on his girlfriend for care

Review the medical record and compare with patient report

profile.title: Worsening Spasticity Eight Months After Spinal Cord Injury: Uncovering Hidden Triggers in a Guarded Patient
profile.summary: A 33-year-old man with chronic complete T10 paraplegia presents by telehealth for worsening leg spasms over three weeks. The case teaches physiatry residents to recognize occult noxious stimuli (UTI, pressure injury, constipation) as drivers of new spasticity, to use remote exam and record review to uncover a reluctantly disclosed pressure injury and under-adherent catheterization despite the patient's sincere belief his routine is unchanged, and to coordinate psychosocial, vocational, and equipment-related referrals within physiatry's scope.
profile.setting: Telehealth video visit, patient at home in Memphis, Tennessee, seated in his wheelchair in his living room
profile.encounterType: Rehabilitation follow-up visit (post-spinal cord injury, spasticity management)
